decks.domain: Occupant protection, steering, braking and blind zones

cards.front: What is the single most effective way to protect yourself in a crash?
cards.back: Wearing a seat belt correctly is the single most effective way to protect yourself and sharply cuts your risk of a fatal injury in a crash.

cards.front: Where should the shoulder belt and the lap belt sit?
cards.back: The shoulder belt goes snugly across the middle of the chest and shoulder, never behind your back, under your arm, or across the neck or face, and the lap belt holds the hips snugly below the stomach.

cards.front: Who in a moving vehicle must be belted or restrained?
cards.back: Under RCW forty-six point six one.six hundred eighty-seven and RCW forty-six point six one.six hundred eighty-eight, all occupants of a moving vehicle need a fastened seat belt or an approved child restraint, and driving or riding without one is illegal.

cards.front: What fit checks do you make for the belt and your seating position?
cards.back: Check that the belt is not twisted, the lap portion sits on the upper thighs and the cross strap falls over mid-shoulder, with knees bending at the seat edge, feet on the floor and headrest in line with your ears.

cards.front: Which three separate fit checks involve the headrest and belt?
cards.back: The headrest lines up with your ears, while the lap belt rests on the upper thighs and the cross strap on mid-shoulder, three separate fit checks.

decks.domain: Occupant protection, steering, braking and blind zones

cards.front: What standards must child restraints meet, and who can check the installation?
cards.back: Child restraints must meet Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards and be installed following both the vehicle and the seat maker's instructions, and a certified child passenger safety technician can check the installation.

cards.front: How long should a child stay in each restraint stage, and how do children ride until age two?
cards.back: Keep a child in each restraint stage as long as that seat allows, and a child from birth until age two must use a car seat that faces the rear.

cards.front: How must children aged two to four ride?
cards.back: Children aged two to four must ride in a car seat with a harness, which may face either rearward or forward.

cards.front: How long do children aged four and older stay in a car or booster seat?
cards.back: Children aged four and older stay in a car or booster seat until the vehicle's lap and shoulder belts fit properly, usually between ages eight and twelve, and the booster stage covers kids from four years old up to a height of four feet nine inches.

cards.front: Who must wear a properly fitting seat belt instead of a booster?
cards.back: Anyone taller than four feet nine inches who is old enough for a seat belt must wear a properly fitting belt.

cards.front: Why must you be belted when airbags deploy, and who should never ride in front?
cards.back: Airbags work together with seat belts, so an unbelted occupant risks serious injury or death when an airbag deploys, and children under thirteen should never ride in the front seat.

cards.front: At what age do the harness stage and the booster stage meet?
cards.back: Children aged two to four ride in a harnessed car seat, while from age four they move to a car or booster seat until the adult belt fits, so the harness stage and the booster stage meet at age four.

cards.front: How does leaving the booster differ from the front-seat rule?
cards.back: Leaving the booster depends on belt fit and a height over four feet nine inches, typically between ages eight and twelve, whereas the front-seat rule is a separate age line of under thirteen.
cards.memory_hook: booster by fit, front by age

decks.domain: Occupant protection, steering, braking and blind zones

cards.front: Where should your hands be on the steering wheel for the best control?
cards.back: For the best control, hold the outside of the wheel on its top half, picturing the wheel as a clock face with hands at about nine and three.

cards.front: When is hand-over-hand steering used, and how is it done?
cards.back: Hand-over-hand steering, starting from nine and three or ten and two, is for low-speed turns, limited visibility, intersections, parking and skid recovery: reach one arm across the other, pull, release the lower hand, and straighten the wheel as the turn ends.

cards.front: When do you use one-hand steering, and when is the twelve o'clock position used?
cards.back: Use one-hand steering when backing up or when you must reach for controls such as wipers, flashers or lights, and the twelve o'clock hand position is recommended only for backing while you turn your body to look behind.

cards.front: Why does hand-to-hand steering never cross the arms?
cards.back: Hand-to-hand steering never crosses the arms and never lets go of the wheel, so the arms stay out of the airbag area and corrections can be made instantly.

cards.front: When is one-hand steering at twelve recommended?
cards.back: One-hand steering with the hand at twelve is recommended only when backing, which differs from the nine and three or ten and two positions used for forward driving.

decks.domain: Occupant protection, steering, braking and blind zones

cards.front: What are the four braking levels?
cards.back: The guide names four braking levels, light, medium, firm and emergency, and judging the right pressure is a skill that grows with practice in your vehicle.

cards.front: What braking should you aim for, and what image helps?
cards.back: Aim to need only light and medium braking, brake as if a cup of water sat in your lap, and avoid needless hard stops that could surprise drivers behind you.

cards.front: What does an antilock brake system do, and not do?
cards.back: An antilock brake system lets you keep steering during an emergency stop but does not shorten your stopping distance, and you may feel the car shake when it engages.

cards.front: Where should you practice firm or emergency braking?
cards.back: Practice firm or emergency braking in a large open paved area to feel the ABS stop the wheels from locking.

cards.front: What does an Antilock Brake System do during emergency braking?
cards.back: An Antilock Brake System lets drivers keep better steering control during emergency braking without shortening stopping distance, and the vehicle may shake slightly when it engages.

cards.front: How should you accelerate?
cards.back: Smooth acceleration follows the same cup-of-water idea, ranging from simply easing off the brake in stop-and-go traffic to speeding up quickly to avoid a hazard.

decks.domain: Occupant protection, steering, braking and blind zones

cards.front: What keeps a vehicle's weight balanced and stable?
cards.back: Keeping weight evenly spread across all tires keeps the vehicle stable, helped by regular maintenance, correct tire pressure and alignment checks.

cards.front: What is pitch, and where does weight go when you accelerate or stop?
cards.back: Pitch is the forward and backward weight shift: accelerating loads the rear of the vehicle, while a sudden stop loads the front.

cards.front: What is roll, and where does the weight go in a left turn?
cards.back: Roll is the side-to-side weight shift, and in a left turn centrifugal force pushes the weight onto the outside, or right side, of the vehicle.

cards.front: What is yaw, and what causes it?
cards.back: Yaw is the zig-zag that happens when you steer sharply from side to side, because the front wheels follow the steering while the rear may slide out of line.

cards.front: How does pitch differ from roll?
cards.back: Pitch shifts weight front to back, so acceleration loads the rear and hard braking loads the front, unlike roll, which shifts weight side to side in turns.

cards.front: In a left turn, which side does the weight roll onto?
cards.back: In a left turn the weight rolls onto the right, or outside, side of the vehicle, not onto the side you are turning toward.

decks.domain: Occupant protection, steering, braking and blind zones

cards.front: What are vehicle reference points used for?
cards.back: Vehicle reference points such as the left headlight, center of the hood, side mirrors and rear bumper help you judge distance when parking, turning, backing and stopping.

cards.front: Where is your front end when the stop line appears under your side mirror?
cards.back: When the stop line appears under your side mirror at an intersection, your front end is roughly three to six inches from that line.

cards.front: Where is your vehicle when the hood center lines up with the lane marking?
cards.back: When the center of your hood lines up with the lane marking, your vehicle is roughly three to six inches from the edge of the lane.

cards.front: What does the side-mirror reference point tell you?
cards.back: The side-mirror reference point is a forward check: with the stop line under the mirror, the front of the vehicle sits about three to six inches from the line.

decks.domain: Occupant protection, steering, braking and blind zones

cards.front: What are blind zones, and who is responsible for what is in them?
cards.back: Blind zones are areas you cannot see from the driver's seat that can fully hide a car, motorcyclist or bicyclist, and you are responsible for knowing what is in them.

cards.front: How do you shrink blind zones?
cards.back: Shrink blind zones by setting the rearview mirror to see out the back window without stretching and setting the side mirrors by the traditional or enhanced method, then still turn your head with the wheel held straight to check.

cards.front: What does a regular scan cover?
cards.back: A regular scan covers the road ahead, the rearview mirror, both side mirrors and over both shoulders.

cards.front: How do you stay out of other drivers' blind zones, and what are no zones?
cards.back: Stay out of other drivers' blind zones by adjusting your speed, and take extra care around buses, motor homes and commercial vehicles, whose large blind zones are called no zones.

cards.front: What does it mean if you cannot see a large vehicle's mirrors?
cards.back: If you cannot see a large vehicle's mirrors, its driver cannot see you.

cards.front: How do you handle other drivers' blind zones?
cards.back: Other drivers' blind zones are handled by speeding up or slowing down until they can see you, and buses, motor homes and commercial vehicles have larger ones called no zones.

cards.front: How often should you check and adjust your mirrors?
cards.back: Recheck and adjust your mirrors every time you get behind the wheel, and keep checking them for changes while you drive.

cards.front: What does a good pre-drive routine check?
cards.back: A good pre-drive routine checks outside the vehicle for tire debris, glass, leaks and obstacles such as children or pets, checks inside for warning lights, clear windows and secured items, confirms mirrors, seat, wheel, belt and a silenced phone, and checks that you feel healthy, focused and calm.

recap_hooks.text: A correctly worn belt is your best protection, and every occupant of a moving vehicle must be belted.
Shoulder belt across mid-chest, lap belt low on the hips and thighs, untwisted, with the headrest at ear level.
Use approved restraints installed to both makers' instructions, and keep each stage as long as the seat allows.
Rear-facing to two, harnessed seat from two to four, then a car or booster seat until the belt fits.
Taller children wear the belt, airbags need belts, and under thirteen ride in back.
Hold the top half of the wheel near nine and three, and use hand-to-hand steering without crossing arms.
Hand-over-hand is for low-speed turns and parking, and one hand at twelve is only for backing.
Know the four braking levels and brake as if a cup of water sat in your lap.
ABS keeps steering but does not shorten stops, so practice it in an open lot.
Balanced weight keeps the car stable.
Pitch is front to back, roll is side to side, and yaw is the zig-zag.
In a left turn the weight rolls to the right.
Reference points help you judge distance; the mirror and hood checks each put you a few inches from the line.
You are responsible for your blind zones, so set mirrors well and still turn your head.
Stay out of others' blind zones, especially large vehicles' no zones.
Recheck mirrors every drive and run a pre-drive routine.

merges.justification: sec04-F12's accepted wording ('hand-to-hand (pull/push) steering') fails the spoken-form card gate (slash symbol); its hand-to-hand steering method (hands at nine and three or ten and two, each on its own side, one pulls while the other slides, never crossing) is carried on the sec04-R04 hand-to-hand steering card, taught in its card script, the lesson and its own exam item.
